Immunotherapies are already curing and extending lives. Diseases that used to be fatal within months have become survivable diseases. Blood Cancer United is the largest private funder of blood cancer research, and our researchers and patients tell us how their lives have changed as a result. This progress isn’t someday. It’s happening right now, and it’s one of the great medical achievements in recent decades.
And yet, the path to this progress is fragile. These breakthroughs took years of sustained research funding and partnerships among government, academia and industry – no single entity can go it alone.
But because of federal cuts, that research is growing less certain by the day. Labs are shutting down mid-study. Young scientists are leaving the field for something more stable. Patients in the middle of a clinical trial are threatened with the prospect of having their treatments taken away. These promising immunotherapies aren’t being held back by science, but rather by a lack of funding.
Prop. 38 would give California the chance to lead the next wave of cancer breakthroughs. By investing in immunotherapy research at leading nonprofit universities and research centers, it would help move promising discoveries from the lab to patients faster. And by requiring researchers to collaborate and share what they learn, Prop. 38 would build a statewide research network focused on one urgent goal: more lifesaving treatments, sooner.
This means new investments will continue in treatments such as chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, commonly known as CAR-T. It continues to revolutionize treatment for cancer.
By reprogramming a patient’s own blood, their T-Cells find and destroy cancer cells. It is often used after other treatments have failed for patients because of its complexities. And it saved Laurie Adami, a blood cancer patient in Los Angeles, after several rounds of chemotherapy and other treatments did not get the lasting results she needed. Not only did CAR-T treatment save her life, but ongoing research has also led to several other FDA-approved CAR-T therapies for cancer.
Prop. 38 will save lives.
And California is uniquely positioned to seize this moment, with some of the country’s most respected and prestigious research institutions and National Cancer Institutes. Collaboration among potential grantees across institutions on discoveries, expertise and best practices can keep the state a leader in innovation and access to treatments for patients.
Prop. 38 is designed to create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines broad competitive funding with a world-class institution capable of accelerating discoveries into lifesaving treatments for patients.
The science is ready. The only question is whether we fund it.
Blood Cancer United stands with every patient and family who has been told to hold on just a little longer for a breakthrough. Patients don’t get to pause their disease while funding cycles run their course, and we can’t afford to pause progress. Prop. 38 is how we get there faster, with more treatments, more cures and more hope.
On behalf of the patients and families we serve, I urge California voters to vote “yes” on Prop. 38.
Dr. Gwen L. Nichols is chief medical officer of Blood Cancer United (formerly The Leukemia & Lymphoma Society).

LOS ANGELES, CA – La Opinión endorsed (https://laopinion.com/2026/10/10/la-opinion-dice-si-a-la-proposicion-38/) Proposition 38 in an October 10 editorial, saying the measure would provide a stable source of support for medical research disrupted by federal funding cuts.
“The purpose of Proposition 38, which California voters are already deciding, is to create a stable resource available to scientists to advance science,” La Opinión’s editorial board wrote. “…We believe that the breakthroughs in disease prevention and treatment–made possible by research funded in this way–are a priority for resuming research that had been stalled by the Trump administration.”
Proposition 38 provides vitally needed funding for immunology and immunotherapy (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) research. Half of the funding will be distributed through competitive grants to nonprofit universities and medical research institutes. The other half would support a nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with a University of California campus.
The editorial also highlights several provisions of the measure: 10 percent of revenue generated by funded therapies would go back to the state to help cover the cost of the bond; treatments developed with the funding would be offered to California patients at a price 20 percent below the national average; and for-profit companies would not be eligible for funding.
The editorial also noted support for the measure from organizations including theALS Association (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/#als-association), the Alzheimer’s Association and the American Nurses Association\California (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/#american-nurses-associationcalifornia). The California Democratic Party (https://yeson38.com/es/lista-de-partidarios/) and theCalifornia Republican Party (https://yeson38.com/2026/10/08/democrats-and-republicans-unite-behind-proposition-38-to-cure-and-prevent-diseases/) also support it.
“La Opinión supports (YES on) Proposition 38 and urges its readers to vote for it,” the editorial concludes.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The proposed UCLA Research Park East Core and Shell Improvements (Core and Shell) project
is the first in a series of phased projects. UCLA Research Park consists of two connected
buildings totaling approximately 1,308,000 gross square feet (gsf) on 9.2 acres. Formerly a
shopping mall, a significant portion of the property was undergoing a conversion to high-
technology office space for a single tenant at the time of acquisition.
Consistent with the Regents’ discussion in November 2023 and approval via interim action in
December 2023, the aim of the UCLA Research Park is to bring together scholars and industry
experts from around the world to foster discovery and innovation, benefiting Southern
California and beyond. Initial occupants of Research Park East would include the California
Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII), the UCLA Quantum Innovation Hub,
and the David Geffen School of Medicine.
The Core and Shell project would retrofit the east building, a three-story facility with two
underground levels, for multi-tenant use, including biomedical research and quantum physics
laboratories, which would be developed in subsequent tenant improvement projects. The purpose
of this item is to advance the Core and Shell project through working drawings, as well as for
the construction of an Advanced Work Phase (AWP). The AWP would include interior and
roof demolition, site and utilities preparation, and procurement of long lead-time equipment.
In May 2025, the Regents approved $19.6 million of preliminary plans funding for the Core and
Shell project, funded from campus funds. Since that time, CIII funds contributed $8,145,000 for
preliminary plans funding, reducing the campus funds to $11,455,000. The Regents are now
being asked to take the following actions: (1) Amend the preliminary plans funding from $19.6
million funded from campus funds to $19.6 million funded from campus funds ($11,455,000)
and CIII funds ($8,145,000); (2) approve working drawings funding for the Core and Shell

Project Background and Context
In December 2023, the campus acquired the former Westside Pavilion shopping mall in Los
Angeles, located two miles south of the Westwood campus, to create UCLA Research Park.
The site spans the southeast and southwest corners of Westwood and West Pico Boulevards,
with Research Park East, a 706,000-gsf building, at 10800 West Pico Boulevard; and
Research Park West, a 602,000-gsf building, at 10850 West Pico Boulevard. The two
buildings are connected by an enclosed pedestrian bridge across Westwood Boulevard. See
Attachment 2 for more information.
An anchor tenant in the UCLA Research Park is the CIII, an independent nonprofit focused
on translational immunology research to advance immunotherapies and create spinoff
companies. CIII will maintain a strong connection with UCLA and UCLA Health through
mutually beneficial lease and affiliation agreements involving shared resources and active
participation from UCLA faculty. It will also collaborate with industry experts and external
institutions through sublease agreements, aiming to establish a leading research and industry
ecosystem addressing a wide range of human health challenges.
UCLA Research Park will be planned and developed in distinct phases.

PROJECT SCOPE AND DESIGN
The Core and Shell project would retrofit a portion of Research Park East for multi-tenant
scientific use, including replacement of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems;
conversion of rooftop parking to mechanical and central plant spaces; floodproofing and
upgrades to loading and service areas; improvements to pedestrian entries, stairs, ramps, and
lobbies; and floodplain mitigation measures, including a watertight storefront and modified
entrances.
Existing partially constructed mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems installed for the
former tenant would be removed and replaced with new systems, including points of
connection for future tenant improvements. New utility shafts with vertical ductwork, smoke
dampers, and chilled- and hot-water risers will serve future tenant mechanical equipment.
Existing rooftop parking would be converted into mechanical penthouses and support spaces
for a new central plant and emergency generators. Lost rooftop and basement parking would
be offset by parking in the adjacent southeast structure, per an existing use agreement, and at
Research Park West.
The basement parking level would be floodproofed to support future vibration- and light-
sensitive programming. An existing at-grade loading dock would be upgraded, and a second
loading dock with back-of-house support space would be added. Construction of the new
service yard would require infilling the ramp and vehicular access to the undersized Level
B2 loading dock. This area would be repurposed as back-of-house support space.
The existing south-side stairs and ramp would be reconfigured to accommodate the future
CIII entrance. The existing paseo connecting West Pico Boulevard to the exterior atrium
would be completed as a new pedestrian entry, with a new lobby for UCLA tenants and
visitors. A new employee lobby at the building center would provide a fully accessible entry
from the adjacent parking structure.
The existing storefront along West Pico Boulevard would be removed to raise the concrete
curb for floodplain mitigation and replaced with a watertight storefront system. Entrances
along Research Park East would also be modified to support future flood barriers.
Upgrades to the electrical switchgear rooms and fire and life safety system upgrades in the
easternmost portion of Research Park East would be completed to support occupancy of the
current project; further development of this portion is subject to planning and future
approvals.
See Attachment 3 for additional information.

ADVANCED WORK PHASE
UCLA is requesting construction funding to begin demolition, along with site and utilities
preparation activities. The proposed scope is targeted to begin in October 2026.
The AWP includes all work necessary for interior and roof demolition to create new floor slab
openings for utility shafts and interior stairs; installation of steel at new floor openings;
disconnecting, rerouting, and/or removing utilities; installation of scaffolding; site excavation
and shoring; tree and site paving removal; and installation of a sound wall for noise mitigation.
This work would be required regardless of the specific design ultimately approved for the
future tenant improvements.
See Attachment 4 for additional information.
In addition, procurement of long lead-time elevator, mechanical, and electrical equipment will
be required. Ordering select equipment early would help with supply chain challenges that
could cause delays. Equipment to be ordered has been confirmed and validated during the
project’s preliminary plans phase.
Funding Plan
The Core and Shell project’s working drawings and AWP construction funding of $34.4 million
are proposed to be funded from campus funds ($18,760,000) and CIII funds ($15,640,000). See
Attachment 1 for additional information. The campus anticipates presenting the total project cost
and funding plan for the Core and Shell project to the Regents in November 2026.
Project Delivery and Schedule
As part of the preliminary planning phase, the campus proposed a UCLA-led Construction
Manager at Risk (CMAR) project delivery method. In September 2024, the Regents authorized
the President or his designee to approve a lease transaction. The Master Lease and Affiliation
agreement between the University and CIII includes provisions that allow CIII to lead execution
of the Core and Shell buildout using a CMAR delivery method. The campus has commenced
negotiating a Work Agreement with CIII. The campus and CIII will contribute a pro-rata share of
funding per the terms of the Lease Agreement.
The proposed CIII/CMAR project delivery model would enable an accelerated schedule and cost
savings by having a single CMAR deliver the Core and Shell and CIII’s tenant improvements.
The Core and Shell project is anticipated to be completed in late 2028.
CONSISTENCY WITH SELECT UC POLICIES AND PRACTICE
The project complies with the UC Policies for Seismic Safety, Sustainability, and Small/Disabled
Veteran Business Enterprises.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures- Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)- giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
PATIENT ADVOCATES, DOCTORS, NURSES AND MEDICAL RESEARCHERS URGE YES ON PROP. 38
Leading patient advocates including the Alzheimer’s Association, Michael J. Fox Foundation, American Nurses Association\ California, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society and Prostate Cancer Foundation all urge YES on PROP. 38 because it could save your life and the life of someone you love.
“I was just weeks away from losing my life when a breakthrough immunotherapy gave me a second chance. Vote YES on PROP. 38 because every family facing a devastating diagnosis deserves this same hope.”
-Laurie Adami, Cancer Survivor and Patient Advocate, Los Angeles
YES ON PROP. 38-TO CURE AND PREVENT DISEASES THROUGH LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY RESEARCH
PROP. 38 accelerates development of breakthrough treatments and cures for the diseases that impact nearly every family. At least half of all funds are specifically dedicated to cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s research.
“Immunology harnesses the body’s immune system to detect and stop diseases. Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to prevent diseases including Parkinson’s, heart disease, diabetes and more.”
-Mark Davis, Ph.D., Member of the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine
“One in nine people over 65 are living with Alzheimer’s, but there are currently no effective cures. YES on PROP. 38 provides real promise to find treatments and cures for the millions of patients and their families living with Alzheimer’s and dementia.”
-Susan Disney Lord, Board Chair of Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
HELPS OFFSET FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS TO MEDICAL RESEARCH
Massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research at nonprofit research institutes and universities, delaying progress toward life-saving cures.
PROP. 38 creates a stable source of funding for breakthrough immunology research. All funds are dedicated exclusively to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes- helping California lead the nation in medical innovation, fostering collaboration among top scientists and universities, and creating tens of thousands of good-paying jobs.
“Immunotherapy is transforming the future of cancer care. PROP. 38 will help accelerate life-saving cures while strengthening California’s role as a global leader in medical innovation.”
-Gina Carithers, President and CEO, Prostate Cancer Foundation
LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS FOR CALIFORNIANS
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through PROP. 38 must be provided to California patients at a 20% DISCOUNT. Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will also reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save the state and families tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
PROP. 38 is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS. Ten percent of revenue from the licensing of successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the costs of the bond, including interest.
PROP. 38 also includes strict accountability requirements, including:
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses
Public Disclosure of Spending
Independent Financial Audits
For-profit corporations are not eligible for grant funding
YES ON PROP. 38: SUPPORTED BY DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES
• ALS Association • Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\California • Blood Cancer United • California Colorectal Cancer Coalition • Liver Coalition • Michael J. Fox Foundation • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • Parkinson Association of Northern California ... and many more.
YES on PROP. 38 could save your life and someone you love. Please, vote Yes.
www.YesOn38.com
Susan Disney Lord , Board Chair
Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
Eugene P. Brandon , Ph.D., Board of Trustees
ALS Association
Dr. Brian Shuch , M.D., Board of Directors Member
Kidney Cancer Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.

PROPOSED LAW
California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
“California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative.”
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
The people of the State of California find and declare all
of the following:
(a) Medical research is on the brink of achieving
transformative breakthroughs in preventing, treating,
and curing some of the most deadly and debilitating
diseases and other health disorders that afflict many
people and their loved ones every day.
(b) The emerging medical research fields of
immunology and immunotherapy offer the promise of
groundbreaking advancements in health science that,
if adequately funded, will lead to an explosion of
scientific progress in treating and preventing a wide
array of the most common medical conditions that kill
and disable Americans year after year.
(c) Immunology and immunotherapy harness the
body’s own immune system to recognize and stop
diseases. In recent years, immunotherapy has proven
to be an effective treatment in fighting cancers like
melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and
lymphomas, and more.
(d) Many doctors and research scientists believe
immunotherapies have the potential to prevent and
cure a whole range of diseases and other health
37
conditions in our lifetime, including cancer, heart
disease, neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s
and Parkinson’s, diabetes, obesity, high blood
pressure, high cholesterol, ALS (Lou Gehrig’s Disease),
HIV/AIDS, muscular dystrophy, and autoimmune
diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and
multiple sclerosis.
38
(e) Given that breakthroughs in immunology can
prevent disease and save lives, supporting immunology
and immunotherapy medical research is a vital priority
in the state’s overall approach to improving public
health and saving and improving lives.
(f) In order to fully develop and take advantage of
these emerging technologies, it is critical that a steady
and reliable source of funding be created so that
sustained research can be pursued uninterrupted by
funding shortages that would otherwise threaten to
disrupt progress and stall the momentum of scientific
breakthroughs.
(g) Public funding of medical research has always
been a central component of advancements in modern
medicine. Of all the new drugs approved by the FDA
between 2010 and 2019, the vast majority of them—
99.4 percent—were the result of publicly funded
research.
(h) California has always been at the forefront of
technological developments and breakthroughs. In
particular, California has long been a leader in the
health sciences, as it is home to many of the most
innovative and prestigious medical research institutes
in the world, as well as having the premier system of
higher education in the country—the University of
California—which houses several world-class medical
schools and health science research centers.
(i) It is incumbent on California to lead the way in the
development of immunotherapies that will yield

enormous benefits in the treatment and prevention of
many of the most persistent and debilitating illnesses
that have so far proved resistant to the more

(j) Besides saving lives, funding the development of
immunotherapies will also save the state and California
families billions of dollars in health care costs by
preventing and curing a range of debilitating diseases
and illnesses.
(k) Immunology and immunotherapy will help expand
California’s biotechnology industry, create good-paying
jobs, generate economic output, and stimulate new
sources of revenue through grant funding, intellectual
property licensing, and private sector investments.
Biotechnology in California has the potential to become
as economically significant in the future as information
technology is today.
(l) Millions of families are hurt every year when
devastating diseases like cancer, heart disease,
Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and diabetes ruin or take the
lives of our loved ones. We owe it to ourselves to invest
in promising immunotherapy research that can prevent
and cure diseases that impact all families.
(m) This is a pivotal moment in the history of medical
science, and California must seize the opportunity to
once again serve as the nation’s leader in innovation,
as it so often has in the past.
SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
It is the intent of the people of the State of California in
enacting this act to achieve all of the following:
(a) Fund a world-class and innovative immunology and
immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the
University of California to harness the power of the
human immune system, cutting-edge science and
technologies, and advanced computing technologies to
create scientific discoveries and next-generation
therapies for the prevention and cure of chronic
diseases, enabling Californians to live longer and
healthier lives.
(b) Award grants only to California-based public and
nonprofit universities and nonprofit medical research
institutions for immunology and immunotherapy
research and expand access to lifesaving therapies and
cures for all Californians, ensuring that no funds are
awarded to for-profit organizations or pharmaceutical
companies.
(c) Fund research, education, and the development of
treatments and therapies for various medical
conditions using immunology-based approaches at
public and nonprofit universities and other nonprofit
medical research facilities with proven track records of
conducting successful research and clinical trials, in
order to help end diseases and other illnesses like
cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s,
diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure, and high
cholesterol in our lifetime.
(d) Dedicate over four billion dollars ($4,000,000,000)
specifically for research related to the prevention,
treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and
Alzheimer’s disease.
(e) Bring together biomedical scientists, disease
modelers, genomic technologists, data scientists,
computational experts, inventors of therapeutics, and
clinical trial innovators from around the globe to
develop preventative vaccines to protect against these
diseases and to formulate treatments and cures for
some of the world’s most chronic and serious medical
conditions.
(f) Select for funding a nonprofit research institute that
is independent, collaborative, and innovative, while still
affiliated with the University of California, in order to
streamline state oversight, cut through bureaucracy
and red tape, and ensure focused, outcome-driven
research.
(g) Fund a nonprofit medical research center that will
ultimately be self-sustaining by reinvesting economic
returns from successful therapeutic development into
new avenues of investigation, thereby creating a
financially independent research facility that will
eventually require no public funding.
(h) Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the
immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to
the state to offset the costs of this act, making this
effectively a loan program and ensuring that the
taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital
research.
(i) Require that any recipient licensing a technology or
drug developed with funds from this act make the
technology or drug available to California patients at a
price that is at least 20 percent below the national
average, ensuring that Californians benefit directly
from their public investment.
(j) Ensure that all research funding disbursed under
this act is subject to strict accountability and
transparency requirements, including a requirement
that 98 percent of all funds be spent for costs related to
medical research and development of cures, a limit on
state government administrative spending to no more
than 2 percent, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public
disclosure of all spending, and independent financial
audits.
(k) Protect and benefit the state budget by funding
research that will significantly lower health care costs
in the future and by providing opportunities for the
state to benefit from revenue resulting from patents
and licensing fees arising from immunology
breakthroughs.
(l) Benefit the California economy by creating high-
paying jobs, biomedical industrial projects, and
potential therapies that will generate new tax revenues
in our state.
(m) Raise the biotechnology and life sciences
industries in California to the status of world leadership
in the emerging field of immunotherapy research and
treatment, strengthening the state’s position as a
global hub for health innovation and economic growth.

An $8.4 billion bond for immunology and immunotherapy research will appear on the November ballot.
Proposition 38, if passed, would allocate half of the bond proceeds to one UC-affiliated nonprofit research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health.
The remaining $4.2 billion would be distributed through grants to California researchers by an Advisory and Accountability Research Council consisting of members appointed by the chancellors of seven UC campuses.
The ballot measure includes requirements for the UC campus hosting the institute to have more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3.5 million outpatient visits annually.
The institute must also contain at least 200,000 square feet of research space and have over $250 million in philanthropic commitments.
The only institute eligible for the bond money is the UCLA-affiliated California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy, which studies immune systems and how to harness a patient's own immune system to fight diseases, according to CalMatters .

# Proposition 38: Borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research
## What does California Proposition 38 do?
Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies.
Half the money would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California.
The other half would be distributed to select public universities and nonprofits.
Drugs created through this research would have to be discounted at 20% for Californians and 10% of any revenue from the drugs would go back to the state general fund.
California’s 2026 midterm elections will be held on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.

Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026.

Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund.
The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent.
The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research.
Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid.

California Prop. 38 to use bond money to fund immunology research with half dedicated to one nonprofit
By
John Ramos
John Ramos

/ CBS San Francisco
Add CBS News on Google (https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cbsnews.com)
In about a week, Californians will be casting their ballots, and among the many initiatives is Proposition 38, which seeks to raise a lot of money for medical research. But beyond the measure itself, there is the broader political question of how the initiative process is being used to support private interests.
Proposition 38, if approved, would sell $8.4 billion in state bonds to raise funding specifically for immunology and immunotherapy research. It specifies that half the funding goes toward cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's research.
"And immunotherapies are the cutting-edge form of medical treatment that harness the body's own immune system to stop these diseases," said Yes on 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. "And so, this bond measure steps in and provides funding for this critical medical research, which is really important right now in the face of federal cuts."
That's the interest of Dr. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist who made his fortune inventing hundreds of surgical devices. But now he's interested in creating something new: a research facility at the former Westside Pavilion shopping mall near the University of California, Los Angeles, called the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
"It's the intention of this institute to have an internal, self-funded incubator accelerator to play 'Shark Tank,' if you will. We're going to have the world's leading immunologists and say, 'Yeah, let's invest in that and start a new company,'" Michelson said at a 2024 symposium about the institute which, at that point, existed only on paper.
"Right now, we are in the phase where we are raising funds," he said. "And philanthropy is one source of that. I really would like to find some business partners."
But it seems those business partners may now be the California taxpayers. Michelson's foundation has funded the campaign to the tune of about $40 million to get Prop. 38 on the ballot. And in the measure's language, it dedicates half the money - $4.2 billion - to a single "unnamed" non-profit. But the criteria for selecting that non-profit was written to exactly match Michelson's new institute, so no other entity in the state could possibly qualify.
Dr. Sarah Hill, political science professor at California State University, Fullerton, analyzes the state's voter initiatives and says bond money is usually reserved for long-lasting infrastructure projects because it incurs debt that lasts for decades.
"And it's bond money being used for research, which is kind of unusual," said Hill. "So, it's unusual policy, and you get this kind of unusual outcome as well, of one non-profit being eligible for half the money."
The other half of the money would be handed out in a traditional, competitive process for those applying for grants to study specific projects. But that wouldn't be the case for the CIII, which critics say would also be exempt from California's public disclosure laws. Servicing the bond debt is expected to take $500-600 million from the state's general fund for 20 years or more.
Dr. Robert Kaplan, a research senior scholar at Stanford University, is concerned that lawmakers will be reluctant to fund any other kinds of medical research when so much is going to only one field of study.
"One of the important things about science is that you need a lot of different people with different ideas," said Kaplan, who authored the opposition statement to the initiative. "And so, there's kind of a marketplace for ideas, where the best minds are competing with one another to get the research funding. And then, they're evaluated on their progress and only those who succeed are rewarded with continuing funding. And that model, there seems to be a lot of discussion in the scientific literature, but that model seems to be the best one."
Ulimately, Prop. 38 will be decided by the voters on the issue of curing disease, but it also may be ushering in a whole new way for those with big ideas and enough resources to use the ballot box to convince the public to pay to make them come true.
"And I think it just raises so many questions about this process. That, at this point in the process, is about who has the money to get it on the ballot and to push for it," Hill said. "It's frustrating to watch."
"That's exactly what you want people to spend their money on, which is curing cancer," said Swanson. "So, we're proud to have gotten funding in that way."
Supporters of Prop 38 say it could end up costing the taxpayer nothing because 10% of any profits from medical breakthroughs would be refunded back to the state. But Kaplan said those kind of monetary benefits are not guaranteed and usually take decades to be realized.

Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

Updated October 28, 2026
Proposition 38 on the 2026 California ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) will provide vitally needed funding to cure and prevent devastating diseases that impact millions of Californians, including cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's (https://yeson38.com/faq/).
Key reasons to vote YES on Prop 38, the Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative:
Helps offset federal cuts to medical research
Prop 38 responds to federal funding cuts and uncertainty (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) that are delaying life-saving medical research.
Dedicated funding for cancer, Alzheimer's and heart disease research
Half of all funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) are dedicated specifically to research into cures for Alzheimer's, cancer and heart disease.
Fosters collaboration between leading scientists and physicians
Grants are overseen by an Advisory Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) of leading scientists, doctors and researchers in the field of immunology.
Mandates strong accountability and transparency
State administrative costs are limited to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), with public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
Designed to pay for itself – including interest
Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest.
Requires 20% discount on treatments and cures for Californians
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) below the national average.

Prop 38 Frequently Asked Questions
What does a YES vote on Prop 38 mean?
A YES vote on Prop 38 means California will support $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology research (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at California universities and nonprofit research institutions to find cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease and other devastating diseases in our lifetime. Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself, with 10% of proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies developed from Prop 38 funding returned to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm). Additionally, California patients will get a 20% discount on the cures it helps create (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
Copy link for this answer Copied!
Where will the research funded by Prop 38 happen?
Medical research funded by Prop 38 will be conducted here in California at leading universities and medical research institutions (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) that are well-qualified to conduct breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research.
That may include University of California campuses, such as UCLA, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, UC San Francisco, UC Irvine, UC Davis, and UC Riverside; private non-profit universities, such as Stanford, USC and Caltech; and non-profit research institutions such as City of Hope, Cedars-Sinai, and Sanford Burnham Prebys, among others.
No funds from Prop 38 can be awarded to pharmaceutical companies or other for-profit corporations. (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
Copy link for this answer Copied!
Will Prop 38 make medical treatments more affordable for Californians?
Yes. Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount below the national average (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf). That affordability protection is written directly into the measure — it’s not optional.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
How will Prop 38 be paid for?
Prop 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers (https://yeson38.com/myths-vs-facts/#can-california-afford). Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
How does Prop 38 ensure oversight and accountability?
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits.

Proposition 38
Borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research
Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies. Half the money would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California. The other half would be distributed to select public universities and nonprofits. Drugs created through this research would have to be discounted at 20% for Californians and 10% of any revenue from the drugs would go back to the state general fund. Philanthropist and medical inventor Gary Michelson put this measure on the ballot.

Summary
Support
Supporters say the potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system. They say the funding is needed because the Trump administration has tried to cut funding for federal health science research.
Oppose
Critics fault the measure for focusing on just one subset of biomedical research rather than a wider array of health research. They also question whether the research that might emerge from this fund can produce commercial drugs, given how hard it is to get a drug approved and bring it to market. They also question why just one nonprofit stands to receive half the money and note that it will add $500 million to $600 million a year in debt payments for 20 years.

Myths vs Facts
Get the facts on Prop 38. Learn what the initiative will do and find answers to some of the most common questions about Prop 38.
Updated October 26, 2026
Can California afford Prop 38?
Fact: Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#accountability). 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go back to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), covering both the principal and the interest of the bonds. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most prevalent diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses for Californians by tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses and lower insurance premiums.
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits. Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on saving lives.
For the millions of families that are facing life-threatening and life-altering diseases that take away our loved ones, we can’t afford NOT to invest in promising cures .
Why does California need Prop 38 when the federal government funds medical research too?
Fact: Prop 38 responds to massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty that are shutting down life-saving medical research (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) at California universities and research institutes. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can’t afford to wait.
Prop 38 creates a stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts to accelerate the pace of discoveries to help the tens of millions of patients fighting cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other debilitating diseases.
Prop 38 will make California a national leader in breakthrough medical research , fostering collaboration between leading California-based universities, scientists and physicians.
Prop 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs . Scientific research has become a critical economic engine in California, and studies show (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf) that each dollar invested in medical research returns three dollars back into our state’s economy.
Does half of Prop 38 funding go to one research institute?
Fact: Half of Prop 38 funding will support a world-class nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California with access to leading scientists, technology, laboratory equipment, patients and clinical trials necessary to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.
The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy will very likely apply for funding and meet qualification requirements. However, state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific named institute (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-12/) but can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. Ultimately, the California Department of Public Health is charged with determining which institute receives the funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm).
Will scientists or politicians decide which research Prop 38 funds?
Fact: Under Prop 38, scientists and researchers oversee a competitive process to ensure the most qualified research with life-saving potential is awarded funding. Prop 38 establishes an Advisory and Accountability Research Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), composed of members from seven University of California campuses and 10 – 15 members from California nonprofit universities and academic and research institutions. Each member of the council will be a physician, scientist or researcher with demonstrated experience in the field of immunology and immunotherapy.
Should the private sector fund this research instead of Prop 38?
Fact: Public funding like Prop 38 is vital to support medical research. More than 99% of new FDA-approved drugs from 2010 to 2019 were built on publicly funded research. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2804378) Prop 38 builds on this proven model by supporting universities and nonprofit researchers to move discoveries from the lab to patients faster and more cost-effectively.
Will the people funding Prop 38 benefit financially?
Fact: Prop 38 is funded by a doctor and philanthropists who will not benefit financially. Only public universities and nonprofit research institutions in California are eligible to receive research funding.
YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocates (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses AssociationCalifornia, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson’s Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, as well as patients, doctors and researchers because it will accelerate life-saving cures. This is a publicly accountable, voter-approved bond.

01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.

A growing coalition says No on Proposition 38.

Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.

What does California Proposition 38 do?
Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies. Half the money would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California. The other half would be distributed to select public universities and nonprofits. Drugs created through this research would have to be discounted at 20% for Californians and 10% of any revenue from the drugs would go back to the state general fund.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
Supporters say the potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system. They say the funding is needed because the Trump administration has tried to cut funding for federal health science research.
Supporter endorsements
American Association of Immunologists
California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)
City of Hope
Michelson Center for Public Policy
Opponents
Arguments against
Critics fault the measure for focusing on just one subset of biomedical research rather than a wider array of health research. They also question whether the research that might emerge from this fund can produce commercial drugs, given how hard it is to get a drug approved and bring it to market. They also question why just one nonprofit stands to receive half the money and note that it will add $500 million to $600 million a year in debt payments for 20 years.
Opponent endorsements

Ballot text
This is how the proposition will appear on the ballot.
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue.

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/)
October 20, 2026 October 20, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)

Courtyard view of the UCLA Research Park under construction in the former Westside Pavilion shopping center in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024. Photo by Brian van der Brug, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
READ NEXT
This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/)
July 31, 2026 August 3, 2026
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
